capabilities.target: customer order refund via payments processor, any order, any amount up to order total

instructions.note: "Use your judgment on partial refunds" grants open-ended discretion over partial refund amounts with no stated ceiling, percentage limit, or escalation path.
"Do not ask for confirmation" relies purely on an instruction to skip any human check before an irreversible financial action; there is no structural gate behind this rule.
"Check the order, then issue the refund" does not define what checking entails (eligibility, fraud signals, prior refunds on the same order), leaving the verification step underspecified.

elements.name: Refund API call to payments processor

controls.name: SSO authentication for support staff requests
Per-staff scoped payment credential (replace shared service account)
Human approval gate for refunds above a monetary or percentage threshold
Per-staff daily aggregate refund cap and rate limit

findings.title: Property: no attributable provenance for refund actions (shared service account, unlogged requester identity)

forecast.watch_signal: A new support tool or integration begins reusing the same shared payments service account, or SSO authentication on staff requests is removed or weakened.

evidence.observation: The agent calls the payments processor with one shared service account used by every support tool, and the processor log records only the service account, amount, and order, not which staff member asked; staff chats are deleted after 7 days, so no record ties a refund back to an individual.

recommendations.action: Record the requesting staff member's identity (not only the shared service account) with every refund transaction, and retain the originating request long enough to support audit and dispute resolution.
Replace the single shared service account with per-staff delegated credentials, or propagate the staff SSO identity through to the payments processor call.

findings.title: Property: no amount, confirmation, or rate limit on irreversible refunds

forecast.watch_signal: The agent is allowed to batch or schedule refunds unattended, or the median number of refund actions per session rises.

evidence.observation: "Use your judgment on partial refunds. Do not ask for confirmation." removes any human check on refund amount or frequency, and cap.issue_refund permits any amount up to the full order total with no stated rate or spend cap.

recommendations.action: Require human approval, reviewing the raw order, amount, and reason, for refunds above a defined monetary threshold or above a defined percentage of order total.
Apply a per-staff daily aggregate refund cap and a per-transaction rate limit, enforced outside the model.

stride_coverage.rationale: The agent has no configure capability and no mechanism in the design to modify its own prompt, tools, or credentials; the only capabilities are order_read and issue_refund, neither of which alters agent configuration.

The artifacts do not state whether order_read access is restricted to orders tied to the staff member's active support ticket or open to the full order database, so the scope of confidential data any one staff member can view cannot be assessed.
The artifacts do not describe transport integrity protections, such as TLS or request signing, for the call from the agent to the payments processor.
The payments processor is the intended recipient of the order and payment data needed to execute the refund it was asked to issue, so this is not disclosure to an unintended party.
The artifacts do not state whether the processor log is append-only or otherwise protected from modification after a transaction is recorded.
The artifacts do not describe access controls on who inside the organization can read the processor log.
The design gives the agent no capability to write to, delete from, or otherwise exhaust the payments processor's own transaction log.
The artifacts do not describe how the integration verifies the payments processor endpoint's identity, such as a fixed API endpoint or certificate pinning.
The payments processor is the external system of record for settlement outside this agent's design boundary; repudiation of receipt by the processor itself is not part of this agent's attack surface.

rating.rationale: Both findings are property findings (missing action provenance and missing spend/confirmation limits) on an irreversible, confidential-data financial capability, which rubric section 5a bases on the I-row of the base matrix (S3 -> high) and caps at high regardless of autonomy modifiers. No declared control earns residual credit against either gap: SSO authentication verifies which staff member can use the support tool, but the shared payments service account and the absence of per-request logging mean no individual-level attribution survives to the processor log, and the prompt explicitly removes any confirmation step with no compensating rate or spend cap. Forecast triggers considered (data_scope_expansion, control_removal, autonomy_increase, longer_task_horizon) do not change the tier because no control is currently credited that could further degrade; both gaps are already present at their capped tier today. The most consequential structural fix absent from the design is the missing refund provenance and credential-scoping control (finding.no_refund_provenance): without it, any future expansion of the input surface so that a less-trusted source reaches cap.issue_refund would create a complete attack path rated critical rather than high, since nothing today severs or narrows that path.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in prompt.md and the runtime notes, not observed runtime behavior; actual staff usage patterns, approval practices, or undocumented controls could differ.

No MCP or tool manifest, IaC, or runtime configuration was provided; the payments processor integration, credential scoping, and any existing rate limits are inferred from the runtime notes prose, so confidence on protocol-level controls is medium to low.
No agent card or system architecture diagram was provided; autonomy level and step or runtime limits were inferred from prompt wording rather than observed configuration.
